clinicalPearls: A self-limiting delay in endogenous immunoglobulin production that prolongs and exaggerates the physiological nadir of IgG seen in infancy, with eventual spontaneous recovery.
Defined by low IgG (often with low IgA) in an infant who has normal B-cell numbers and, importantly, retains the ability to make specific antibody to vaccines.
Most children are healthy or have only mild recurrent upper respiratory and ear infections; some present with atopic features such as eczema or wheeze.
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion and can only be confirmed retrospectively once immunoglobulin levels normalise, typically within the first few years of life.
Preserved specific antibody responses (for example to tetanus or conjugate vaccines) are the key feature separating it from true antibody-deficiency syndromes.
B-cell numbers and T-cell function are normal, distinguishing it from agammaglobulinaemia and combined immunodeficiencies.
Routine immunoglobulin replacement is usually unnecessary; management is watchful monitoring with prompt treatment of infections and, occasionally, antibiotic prophylaxis.

Persistent hypogammaglobulinaemia beyond early childhood or failure of specific antibody responses should prompt re-evaluation for common variable immunodeficiency or another primary immunodeficiency.
reference.pathophysiology: Transient hypogammaglobulinaemia of infancy represents a maturational lag rather than an intrinsic structural defect of the immune system. All infants experience a physiological trough in serum IgG as transplacentally acquired maternal IgG is catabolised over the first months of life before endogenous synthesis takes over. In affected infants, the onset of adequate independent IgG (and often IgA) production is delayed, deepening and prolonging this nadir. B lymphocytes are present in normal numbers and are intrinsically capable of maturing into antibody-secreting plasma cells, and the capacity to mount protective specific antibody responses is generally retained, which is why most children remain well or only mildly symptomatic. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve delayed maturation of T-cell help, transient dysregulation of cytokines supporting immunoglobulin class-switching, or slow expansion of the memory B-cell compartment. Because the underlying machinery is intact, immunoglobulin concentrations rise into the normal range as the child grows, distinguishing the condition from the fixed defects of agammaglobulinaemia and from the progressive humoral failure of common variable immunodeficiency, with which it can initially be confused.
additionalDifferentials: Specific antibody deficiency with normal immunoglobulins
Physiological immunoglobulin nadir of normal infancy
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) interpreted against age-matched ranges
Specific antibody titres to protein and polysaccharide-conjugate vaccines
Lymphocyte subsets confirming normal B-cell numbers
Isohaemagglutinin titres as a measure of IgM antibody function
Response to a booster immunisation where specific titres are borderline
Exclusion of protein-losing enteropathy or nephrotic-range protein loss
Longitudinal follow-up to document spontaneous normalisation
redFlags: Severe, invasive or opportunistic infection out of keeping with a benign transient process
Failure to thrive or chronic diarrhoea suggesting a more serious immunodeficiency
Absent specific antibody responses despite adequate immunisation
Persistently low immunoglobulins continuing well beyond early childhood
Very low or absent circulating B cells on immunophenotyping
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution and normalisation of immunoglobulin levels in the majority during early childhood. A minority who fail to recover or lose specific antibody responses may ultimately be reclassified as having a persistent primary immunodeficiency.
pitfalls: Diagnosing it prematurely and definitively when only prolonged follow-up can confirm resolution
Starting unnecessary immunoglobulin replacement in a child with preserved specific antibody responses
Failing to reassess a child whose hypogammaglobulinaemia persists, thereby missing evolving common variable immunodeficiency
Interpreting low immunoglobulins without checking functional specific antibody titres
Overlooking secondary causes such as protein loss before labelling the process transient
